name: Luchazi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: The stress regularly falls upon the penultimate (next to the last) syllable, except in some foreign words. As a rule, the addition of a suffix causes the accent to move forward to the new penult. This is called rhythmic stress as compared with the former, which is called etymological stress. However, the addition of the locative and other enclitic suffixes does not change the stress except in the negative conjugation. In the latter the addition of the enclitics causes the stress to move to the preceding syllable. Example: nja vuíleko — ka nja vuiléko. In the case of monosyllabic verbs, the accent falls upon the preceding monosyllable. Example: u ye. The monosyllabic adverbs always receive the accent. Example: ci vuka tó. ... [The Verb §3] Most primary verbs are disyllabic or trisyllabic and the stress accent falls on the penultimate. Some homonyms are distinguished by musical accent and prolonged vowels. There are about two dozen monosyllabic verbs and in these the stress accent falls on the preceding pronoun or particle.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (stress) accent falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word; adding a suffix moves it to the new penult; locative and other enclitics do not move it except in the negative conjugation, where it retracts one syllable; monosyllabic verbs throw the stress onto the preceding monosyllabic pronoun/particle, and monosyllabic adverbs are always stressed. Tone ('semantic tone'/'musical accent') is a separate, lexically and grammatically distinctive system not tied to the stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; Pearson only says that in most European languages 'the elementary and secondary [accents] are the only ones usually indicated' and that this is insufficient for Luchazi; he describes a 'weak musical accent' (tone) on the ultima when a strong musical accent falls on the antepenult/preantepenult.
new_statements.exceptions: 'except in some foreign words'; negative-conjugation forms with enclitics shift stress back one syllable (ka nja vuiléko); monosyllabic verbs put the accent on the preceding monosyllable (u ye); monosyllabic adverbs are always accented (ci vuka tó); imperative singular and locative demonstratives often accent the final syllable; emphatic/calling forms lengthen and accent the final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, including affixed verb forms with enclitics (nja vuíleko / ka nja vuiléko) and clitic groups (monosyllabic verb + preceding pronoun/particle: 'u ye'). Pearson explicitly separates this dynamic stress from 'semantic tone' ('musical accent'), which distinguishes homographs and tenses and often falls on a different syllable, even the antepenult or preantepenult, with a weak musical accent on the ultima. So Luchazi is described as a tone language with an independent, regular penultimate dynamic stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Pearson's grammar describes the Luchazi of the Muié area (Moxico, eastern Angola), the variety he also calls 'Ngangela' (his 1970 Ngangela-English dictionary is mapped by Glottolog to Luchazi [lch]/Mbunda). This is luch1239 proper (K.13), NOT the Nyemba/Ngangela of Menongue (nyem1238, K.12b) described by Maniacky 2003 and Zavoni Ntondo 2003, which is already in the catalog. Caveat: the deciding text is a 2018 blog transcription by a community member (Kalenga Chihinga) of an undated missionary grammar held by the Africa Evangelical Fellowship; the transcriber states the original's integrity was preserved but that definitions and tables were added (the dictionary-style opening sentence of the 'Accent' section looks like such an addition; the stress rule itself reads as Pearson's).
